As someone who is planning on getting a bachelors in cyber security and currently has an associates in information technology, yes please. ELI5!

IT guy here, but networking isn't my specialty, so take this with a GIANT grain of salt...

A bunch of people, like a flash mob, suddenly show up to the same store and demand service from the person at the registers. The store opened more registers, but remains overwhelmed by the number of people. The store manager sees that not everyone who showed up to the registers actually wants to buy things.

Some showed up wearing "I'm here to break stuff!!!" t-shirts. They were immediately kicked out by the manager (obvious malicious traffic).

Some people showed up, filled a basket with random things, stuck the basket in line and left. The store manager sees this, and moves the baskets out of line. (Packet flooding, usually attacks on infastructure. No source (or known bad source) found in the packet, the packet gets dropped rather than opened and processed).

Some just want to stand there and take up the cashiers time by asking for a price check, then wander back into the store and get back in line to repeat the process. The store manager doesn't like this, of course, so he's now setting up lane checkers, who walk through the lines asking if people are actually buying things or looking for price checks. These lane checkers find out who the real customers are, and direct them to proper lines, while kicking the price checkers out. (Layer 4 and up attacks I think, where packets have to be opened and processed, but can be dropped or removed if something doesn't look right)

The lane checkers can become overwhelmed though, having to go through each line. So they begin forming one line, where they can more rapidly check each person's purpose. This sorts the real buyers from fake buyers.

Now, some real buyers still ask for price checks as they get through, but the cashier can make the choice of calling them out of line while handling other customers, or actually completing the price check if it's quick enough. (application layer packet checking, or layer 7. Packets that make it this far have met whatever stringent requirements were necessary to get through the other layers 2-6, so fewer packets make it this far and keep the application from being overwhelmed. Packets still get dropped if they appear to be malformed / incorrect)

Anyways, that's the overall 5 year old version.
